w: Nikola Tesla's ashes rest here, in an urn inside a museum that displays barely a fraction of what it owns - 160,000 documents and 1,200 technical exhibits sit catalogued behind the scenes, while the small ground-floor gallery shows only a sliver. That archive made UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2003.
s: Tesla's own archive, and his final resting place
_facts: Science museum dedicated to Nikola Tesla's life and work, and his final resting place
Holds over 160,000 documents, 1,200 technical exhibits and 1,000 plans/drawings; little is on display
The Nikola Tesla Archive was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2003

w: Two brutalist towers joined by a sky-bridge and a revolving restaurant that never once revolved - Mihajlo Mitrovic's 1977 gateway held the title of Serbia's tallest building for 42 years. One tower is still lived in; the other, once a state trading company's HQ, stands empty.
s: A brutalist gateway with a restaurant that never spun
_facts: 36-story brutalist skyscraper designed by Mihajlo Mitrovic in 1977, also called the Western City Gate
Two towers linked by a bridge with a revolving restaurant that was never operational
Tallest building in Serbia for 42 years until 2021
One tower, formerly Genex Group HQ, now stands empty; the other remains residential

w: Serbia's oldest museum, founded in 1844, took over a century to find its permanent home on Republic Square - the collection didn't move in until 1950, and the building didn't formally open until 1952. It's grown since to more than 400,000 objects, and now carries protected status as a Monument of Culture.
_facts: Largest and oldest museum in Belgrade, established 10 May 1844
Moved into its present Republic Square building in 1950, formally opened 1952
Collection has grown to over 400,000 objects
Declared a Monument of Culture of Great Importance in 1979

w: Originally intended as the parliament of the Kingdom of Serbia, this domed building on Nikola Pasic Square outlived that kingdom entirely - going on to house the Assembly of Yugoslavia, then of Serbia and Montenegro, and since 2006 the National Assembly of Serbia. Three vanished states, one dome.
s: One parliament building, three vanished states
_facts: Seat of the National Assembly of Serbia, on Nikola Pasic Square
Originally intended as the House of the National Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbia
Also served as the seat of the Assembly of Yugoslavia and the Assembly of Serbia and Montenegro
Has been the National Assembly of Serbia's meeting place since 2006

w: Uninhabited and named for wars long past, Great War Island rises exactly where the Sava meets the Danube - wild river land that officially belongs to Belgrade City, under the municipality of Zemun, despite having nobody living on it.
s: An uninhabited island where two rivers meet
_facts: River island at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers
Uninhabited
Administratively part of Belgrade City, in the municipality of Zemun

w: Built in 1964 as headquarters for the Communist Party's Central Committee, this tower overlooking the Sava-Danube confluence was hit hard by NATO airstrikes on 21 April 1999. Reconstructed from 2003 with two extra floors, it's now just office space for rent - its twin, added in 2020, completes the pair.
s: A bombed Communist HQ, rebuilt as office space
_facts: Built 1964 as headquarters of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia
Severely damaged by NATO airstrikes on 21 April 1999
Reconstructed from 2003 with two added floors and an antenna; now commercial office space
A twin tower was completed in 2020

w: Cable-stayed off a single pylon at the tip of Ada Ciganlija island, this bridge split opinion before a car had crossed it - critics called it megalomaniacal, boosters called it the most beautiful bridge in Belgrade. Since 2012 it's become inescapable, the backdrop of choice for music videos and commercials alike.
s: The bridge that split Belgrade before it even opened
_facts: Cable-stayed bridge over the Sava River, pylon at the tip of Ada Ciganlija island
Connects Čukarica and New Belgrade, opened 1 January 2012
Design was polarizing among professionals and politicians before construction
Became a widely used symbol of Belgrade, appearing frequently in music videos and commercials

w: Founded in 1958 as the Modern Gallery - one of the first museums of its kind anywhere - Belgrade's contemporary art museum spent a decade shuttered for renovation before reopening in 2017. The Usce building itself, by architects Ivan Antic and Ivanka Raspopovic, is as much the exhibit as the 35,000 works inside.
_facts: Founded 1958 as the Modern Gallery, among the first museums of its kind
Moved to its current Usce, New Belgrade building in 1965
Building designed by architects Ivan Antic and Ivanka Raspopovic
Collection of over 35,000 works of Serbian and Yugoslav art since 1900; closed for renovation 2007-2017
